newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan urges schools to protect kids after murder.
newsitem.headline: Japan urges schools to protect kids after murder.

text.p: A Japanese cabinet minister on Thursday urged educators to take precautions to protect children from serious crimes following the killing and beheading of an 11-year-old boy that horrified the nation.

"Crimes could happen in your school areas and local regions. I would like to ask you to take necessary steps to secure the safety of children, such as checking possible dangerous areas," Education Minister Takashi Kosugi was quoted by Kyodo news agency as telling an emergency meeting of school board representatives from around the nation.

The killing and beheading of schoolboy Jun Hase in the city of Kobe in central Japan last month sent shockwaves across a country which has prided itself on a low level of crime and where young children often walk through city streets alone.
Parents of elementary schoolchildren typically form small groups to patrol city streets once or twice a year on the lookout for potential trouble.
Hase's murder, however, sparked worries that the tight social networks which have kept crime low are unravelling.
"For their part, communities must become more vigilant so they may nip crime in the bud," said one newspaper editorial after the murder.

The boy left his home in a Kobe suburb shortly after noon on May 24, saying he was going to see his grandfather. Three days later his head was found in front of the iron gate of a nearby junior high school.
Inside the boy's mouth was a note which said the murderer enjoyed killing and planned to strike again.
Earlier this month, a person purporting to be the killer sent a letter to a local newspaper blaming Japan's draconian education system for his murderous urges.
A National Police Agency report released on Thursday showed crimes against younger children are on the rise, Kyodo said.

The agency said the number of elementary school children who fell victim to crimes rose 11.6 percent to 23,720 in 1996, the second consecutive annual increase. Among the crimes, kidnappings jumped 31.2 percent to 101.
